names.name: Brahman — beginningless, supreme, imperishable (anādimat paraṃ brahma; akṣara)
Puruṣottama, the highest person beyond the perishable and the imperishable
Paramātman, the supreme self in the body
Īśvara / Maheśvara, the Lord dwelling in the heart of all beings
the twenty-sixth, the awakened (buddha), beyond the twenty-five

descriptions: beginningless supreme Brahman, said to be neither being nor non-being (BhG 13.12)
with hands and feet everywhere, eyes, heads and faces everywhere, it stands enveloping all (13.13)
the light of lights beyond darkness, knowledge, the known and the goal of knowledge, seated in the heart of all (13.17)
that by which all this is pervaded is indestructible (2.17)
the highest Person who, entering the three worlds, sustains them (15.17–18)
the origin and dissolution of the whole world; all this is strung on him like pearls on a thread (7.6–7)
the knower of the field in all fields (13.2)
the twenty-sixth, ever awake, which the twenty-fifth comes to know (MBh 12.294–296)
negations: neither being nor non-being — na sat tan nāsad ucyate (BhG 13.12)
weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it (2.23–24)
not seen with the ordinary eye, nor by Vedas, sacrifice, study or austerity, but by a divine eye or undivided devotion (11.8, 11.48, 11.53–54)
all beings abide in me but I do not abide in them — and yet beings do not abide in me (9.4–5)
the sun, moon and fire do not illumine that supreme abode (15.6)
relation_to_self: The self in every body is unborn and eternal (BhG 2.20); the Lord is the knower of the field in all fields (13.2) and an eternal portion of him becomes the living being (15.7); the supreme person in the body is witness, permitter, supporter and experiencer (13.22). The Mokṣadharma distinguishes the twenty-fifth (the self coming to awakening) from the twenty-sixth (the awakened) and teaches that the knower attains oneness (12.294–296). The commentators read these relations as identity (Advaita), the Lord as inner self of the selves (Viśiṣṭādvaita) or eternal difference (Dvaita).
relation_to_world: The Lord's lower, eightfold nature (earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect, ego) and his higher nature, the life-element, are the womb of all beings (BhG 7.4–6); at the end of each kalpa beings enter his prakṛti and at its beginning he sends them forth, prakṛti producing the moving and unmoving under his oversight (9.7–10); the world of saṃsāra is an aśvattha tree rooted above (15.1–3); he descends age after age to protect dharma (4.7–8).
caveat: The epic milieu is plural: it records Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Vedic, Pāñcarātra and Pāśupata views (MBh 12.337.59), differing counts of principles, and the question whether puruṣas are many or one (12.338). BhG 12.1–5 holds that worshippers of the unmanifest imperishable and of the Lord in form both reach him, the former with greater difficulty. Each Vedānta school reads the Gītā's ultimate in its own way and rejects the others' readings; the one-truth reading belongs to the interpretation layer, not to the epic's own text.

descriptions: Vāsudeva the Lord is the knower of the field, whose self is without guṇas (MBh 12.326.38)
the fourfold form (caturmūrti): Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha (12.326.68–69, 12.326.93)
the dwelling of all (sarvāvāsa), the supreme self entered by the liberated (12.332.17)
the culmination (niṣṭhā) of every system of knowledge (12.337.63–64)
the one who appears again and again to protect the worlds (12.326.71–94)
negations: not seen by those without one-pointed devotion; even Brahmā has not had such a sight (12.326.96)
relation_to_self: The individual self is Saṃkarṣaṇa, arising from Vāsudeva (12.326.38, 12.326.68); the liberated enter Vāsudeva through the sun and the vyūhas, the ekāntins directly (12.332.13–18; 12.336.3).
relation_to_world: From Aniruddha comes Brahmā, from Brahmā all moving and unmoving beings, at the beginning of each kalpa (12.326.69–70); the Lord withdraws the world at the end of a thousand ages and dwells alone with knowledge (12.326.66–67).
caveat: Described both as the Lord with a form and as without guṇas; the later schools that inherit this devotion (Pāñcarātra, Viśiṣṭādvaita, Dvaita, Gauḍīya) reject an impersonal reading of it, while Advaita readers take the personal Lord as Brahman with attributes. The Nārāyaṇīya itself records the Pāśupata system as a distinct knowledge (12.337.59, 62) and states that Rudra and Nārāyaṇa are one being made twofold (12.328.24).
